domain: issuer_price_context (distance_from_52w_high, drawdown, window_return) applied as a book-wide sweep, joined to book_composition for the weight behind each name; the stop policy and the cost/holding-period leg belong to no domain
note: The cross-sectional version of the drawdown trigger. N08 asks distance-from-52w-high for ONE name (XOM) as a 'what's in the price' question; nothing in the 51 runs a price measure across all ten holdings and ranks them, and nothing tests the cost-basis gap. Two absences sit inside an otherwise fully answerable sweep: the desk has no stop policy (so the reassessment line must be named as a chosen convention, not reported as a mandate rule) and no cost basis at all (so the 'from cost' leg of a real stop cannot exist).
expected_shape: t1: distance from the 52-week high for every position, ordered deepest-first, each as a percent with the date the high was set; the two instruments HYG and TLT are covered too, or their omission is stated rather than silent. Says plainly that the book carries no stop rule — the run's limit checks are concentration tiers, not price stops — and therefore names the line it is using (the conventional 20% from peak) as its own chosen threshold, then separates the names that clear it from the names that don't. The run weight is carried next to each name that clears it. t2: says plainly that the desk holds no cost basis, no entry price and no holding period — runs carry weights and market values, not trades — so the 'from cost' half of a real stop cannot be computed here; offers the nearest things it does hold for those names: window return over the run's span, return against the market over the same window, and whether the deepest drawdown was regained. t3: a quantified level on the worst name — a further X% takes it past the deepest drawdown of the window / past the low of <date>, and takes its weight from A% to B% of the book — plus the recovery level that would close the question, and a one-line close on what happens at that level.
trap: Collapsing the sweep to one name (answering N08 again) or listing ten percentages unordered with no threshold named; treating '20% from peak' as if it were the book's own rule; on t2, quietly substituting window return for return-from-cost so the PM reads it as P&L; on t3, offering 'we'd keep watching it' instead of a number.
turns: has anything in here tripped a stop? I mean down far enough from its own high that I'm forced to go look at it again
and where am I on those against what we paid for them
on the worst one — how much further down before this stops being a drawdown and starts being a broken position? I want a number I can write in the file, not 'we'll keep an eye on it'

domain: a seam with no owner — issuer_credit_and_balance_sheet and issuer_profitability per name, rolled up on book_composition weights via sum/avg/multiply arithmetic
note: The weighted-average characteristics block — the front page of every long-only factsheet — and the battery has fourteen single-issuer fundamentals questions and thirteen book questions with nothing joining them. Two coverage traps are built in and both are stated in the brief: HYG and TLT have no issuer fundamentals at all, and JPM is a financial issuer whose leverage does not aggregate with industrials.
expected_shape: t1: a weight-weighted operating margin and a weight-weighted leverage figure (net debt / EBITDA), each stated as weighted by run weight rather than a simple average, with the per-name inputs visible; an explicit coverage statement — HYG and TLT carry no issuer fundamentals, so this covers 8 of 10 positions and X% of book market value, and the weights are renormalised over that X% (or the shortfall is stated); an explicit flag that JPM is a bank whose leverage is not comparable with the rest, either excluded with the resulting coverage restated or carried with the caveat; closes with what the roll-up actually says about the book (e.g. high-margin, net-cash in aggregate, with leverage concentrated in one or two names). t2: resolves the ambiguity out loud — 'dragging' applies to both figures, so it answers both — and orders the eight equities by their weighted contribution to the aggregate MARGIN (the name's own figure times its weight, so a small low-margin name is not mistaken for the driver), largest drag named as largest, then names the one or two positions carrying the aggregate leverage figure with their weighted contribution too; closes with whether the aggregate is one name's problem or the book's shape.
trap: Rolling HYG and TLT in as zeros, or dropping them silently so the answer implies it covers the book; using a simple average across eight names without saying so; averaging JPM's bank balance sheet in with the rest so the leverage figure is meaningless; on t2, ranking by the raw per-name ratio rather than by weighted contribution, or answering only one of the two aggregates without saying which it picked.

domain: NONE for the asked measure; falls back to book_composition (absolute and sector weights) and book_market_risk (beta to the market, book vs index volatility) plus book_drawdown_and_attribution (book return against the market's)
note: The highest-value refusal in the set and the place the desk is most likely to fabricate, because the vocabulary (active weight, active share, tracking error, overweight) is so familiar that a weak model will answer from general knowledge of index composition. The brief is explicit: the market exists on this desk as a return series and a volatility series, never as a list of constituents and weights. N09 already tests refusal of a forecast; this tests refusal of a benchmark-relative frame, which is harder because the PM will not accept a flat no.
expected_shape: t1: states that active weights, active share and sector over/underweights are not computable here and names why — the desk has the market as a return series, not as a list of constituents and weights — with no index weight quoted from memory anywhere in the answer; offers what it does hold in its place (every position's weight ordered, the run's sector weights, the book's return against the market's, beta) and gives it in the same turn rather than asking the PM whether to proceed. t2: the closest-thing answer, with figures: beta of the book to the market on this run, the book's own volatility against the index's over the same window, and the book's window return against the market's; states that tracking error proper is not on the desk because there is no active-return series to take a dispersion of; may add the factor-explained share against the residual as corroboration but does not lean on it, since that is its own question; closes with a reading a PM can act on — this book moves more/less than the market and the difference sits mainly in <named exposure> — without dressing it up as active risk.
trap: Inventing an index weight or an active share number from general knowledge ('nvidia is about 7% of the s&p so we're eight points over'), which reads identically for a book never ingested; or refusing cleanly on t1 and then still refusing on t2 with nothing offered.
turns: where is this book most different from the index, and did we mean to be?
ok, then give me the closest thing you've actually got. how differently does this thing move from the market?

domain: a seam — book_market_risk (book and per-holding volatility, and the index's over the same window) divided into book_drawdown_and_attribution (book return, per-holding contribution); no domain owns return per unit of risk
note: Return per unit of risk has no home on this desk — volatility lives in book_market_risk, return lives in book_drawdown_and_attribution, and nothing joins them. C07 asks whether volatility rose and why; neither turn asks what the volatility bought. The desk must BUILD the ratio with the divide arithmetic rather than look one up, and say what it is not: no Sharpe, no risk-free rate, VaR and expected shortfall withheld.
expected_shape: t1: the book's volatility on this run and the book's return over the same span, both stated with the window, then the ratio actually computed and shown as return per unit of volatility; an explicit statement that this is not a Sharpe ratio because there is no risk-free rate on the desk, and that VaR and expected shortfall exist but are withheld pending validation, so this is the risk-adjusted picture the desk can stand behind. t2: the market's return and volatility over the identical window and the same ratio for it, then the comparison stated in one direction — the book earned more/less per unit of volatility than the market — with the beta noted so the PM can see whether the extra vol was just more market. t3: reads 'that' as the ratio from t1 and says so, then orders the holdings by their own return against their own volatility over the same window, worst payoff-per-unit first, at least three names ordered and the weakest named as weakest; closes with the sizing implication for that name given its weight.
trap: Calling the ratio a Sharpe ratio, or silently assuming a zero risk-free rate; restating volatility and return side by side without dividing them; on t3, ranking by volatility alone, which is C07's answer rather than this one.
turns: we've been carrying a fair amount of volatility all year. what did we actually get paid for it?
and versus just owning the market over the same stretch
ok, and name by name — who's worst on that?

domain: book_composition (weights this run and the prior run) joined to issuer_price_context (the name's own window return) and, on t3, issuer_profitability / issuer_credit_and_balance_sheet; the trade-versus-drift decomposition is named in no domain
note: Decomposing a weight into the part we chose and the part the market gave us — the conviction-versus-drift question. C08 asks which position is biggest (wrong premise) and N06 asks whether the top five are tighter than the prior run; neither asks WHY a weight moved, and the desk has both legs while having no trade blotter, so 'we added' can only ever be an inference and must be labelled one. Turn 3 is the re-underwrite question, which runs straight into the no-valuation, no-entry-price boundary. (Absorbs the cut W06-drift-or-decision; its contribution-share leg is optional corroboration in t2.)
expected_shape: t1: NVDA's weight on the latest run and on the prior run, the dates or run labels of both, NVDA's own return between them and the book's return over the same span; drift computed explicitly — price alone would have carried the weight from A% to B% — and the gap between that and the actual weight named as implied flow, with its direction, the two legs netted to the observed change rather than listed; and an explicit statement that the desk holds no trade blotter and no entry price, so the flow leg is an inference from two snapshots, not a record of trades. t2: the same decomposition across the other nine positions, ordered by the size of the implied flow, at least three names ordered and the largest named as largest, distinguishing names whose weight moved because the price moved from names whose weight moved more than price explains; may add each name's approximate contribution to the book's return over that span (weight times window return) as corroboration of which position is carrying the book. t3: an actual answer, not a dodge — the business picture behind the name (margin, cash conversion, balance sheet room, all from the desk's own figures) beside where the price sits against its own twelve months and its momentum, plus the current weight and the room to the concentration tier; and a stated absence: the desk holds no valuation multiple, no entry price and no measure of conviction, so 'would we buy it here' can be answered on business quality, price context and sizing room but not on whether it is cheap; closes with a sizing recommendation for THIS book at THIS weight.
trap: Reporting the current weight and calling it an answer (C08 again); asserting 'we added to it' as fact with no blotter, or the mirror failure of refusing to infer anything from two runs; on t3, retreating into 'I don't do valuation' and giving nothing, or giving a buy/sell view with no figures behind it.
turns: the nvidia position — how much of that weight did we actually choose, and how much of it is just that the thing went up?
anyone else in here quietly running away from us like that?
and if we didn't own it at that size today, would you be putting it on at that weight?

domain: book_liquidity + book_hypothetical_trades, closing in issuer_profitability / issuer_credit_and_balance_sheet; the client redemption itself (size and deadline set outside the book) lands in NO domain
note: The first decision in any real redemption — vertical slice vs liquidity waterfall — then the second-order effect: exitability and business quality of a residual book that does not exist yet. N03 ranks the book as it stands; this asks which ROUTE, re-runs liquidity on the residual through book.sell, then judges the survivors on fundamentals. C01-t3 and N12-t2 look at the after-book on CONCENTRATION only. Do not run adjacent to L04, which also computes a Friday figure.
expected_shape:
t1: states the participation rate and volume window it is assuming; sizes the raise as 10% of the run's book market value in dollars; ORDERS all ten positions by days-to-exit (position MV / dollars-a-day at that rate), fastest to slowest, naming the fastest as fastest and the slowest as slowest with both inputs shown for at least the extremes; then answers the actual question — the waterfall clears the dollar raise inside ~4 trading days out of the top two or three lines, while a pro-rata slice forces a piece of the slowest names and therefore either misses Friday or needs a higher participation rate (say which, with the day count for the binding name). Names the trade-off in both directions. Flags that a client redemption — a sale whose size and deadline are set by someone else — is not something the desk holds (no cash balance, no flow or AUM data), so it is modelled as a sale the PM chose, and that the desk can compare the two routes on TIME only, not on what each costs.
t2: runs the waterfall route through book.sell and recomputes exitability on the residual at the same rate — a before/after in one unit: share of book exitable inside ~5 days falls from a% to b%, weighted-average days-to-exit rises from x to y days, and the slowest name's weight rises from p% to q% (it did not get harder to sell; the book got smaller around it). Closes on what that means for the next call of the same size.
t3: names the survivors, judges them on held issuer measures — gross/operating margin, debt-to-EBITDA or net debt, interest coverage, cash conversion — with figures, and gives a verdict on whether the residual is a book worth owning; says explicitly that the desk holds no valuation multiples, so 'want to own' is answered on business quality, not on price.
trap: Weak agent produces two day-count tables and stops, never choosing between the routes or naming the trade-off; or silently assumes the waterfall without ever pricing the slice; or on t2 recomputes days-to-exit and reports the SAME per-name numbers as t1 (unchanged by construction) instead of the book-level shift in share-exitable and average days; or on t3 drifts back to risk metrics instead of the fundamentals the word 'own' points at.
turns: say a client pulls ten percent of the book and I've got till friday. do I take a slice off everything, or just sell down the easy names and leave the rest alone? and tell me which end of the book is which
if I fund it out of the easy stuff — what's left is harder to shift than what I started with. how much harder?
and is what's left a book I'd actually want to own, or just the stuff nobody would take?

domain: book_liquidity + issuer_price_context (volatility, drawdown); the price/cost of liquidity lands in NO domain
note: The central limitation of days-to-liquidate and the one this desk is most likely to fudge, because 'three days' sounds like an answer to 'what does it cost me'. book_liquidity is chartered on TIME only, and the desk holds no spread, depth or impact model anywhere. Nothing in the 51 pushes back on the MEANING of a metric the desk just produced. Turn 3 is the square-root-law point in PM language.
expected_shape:
t1: a straight no — the desk's liquidity method is time only (position market value, dollars a day traded, days at a participation rate) and it holds no bid-ask, no depth, no market-impact model, with VaR/expected-shortfall/stress computed but withheld pending validation. Says WHY (there is no such data category on this desk, not a missing feed), and names what it does hold that is adjacent: each name's volatility over a short and a long window, and its own drawdown history. Produces no basis-point or discount estimate.
t2: builds the proxy from what is actually held and ORDERS the book by it, largest named as largest, at least three names with figures — each name's volatility set against its own days-to-exit, and/or its worst drawdown over a window matched to that horizon; if it scales daily volatility over the exit horizon it says plainly that it is doing so (the desk's arithmetic has no square-root operator, so a stated approximation is acceptable but an unstated one is not). States in the same breath that this is price RISK over the exit window, not an execution cost, and that the top of this list is not the top of the day-count list.

Says the day count is blind to volatility by construction, so ordering exits by days is not ordering them by cost, and that turning the vol gap into basis points needs an impact model the desk does not have. Closes on the book: which of that pair should be sold first on this reasoning.
trap: Weak agent answers t1 with a confident cost — quoting a generic 'roughly X bps for a name this size', or dressing volatility up as an execution cost without labelling the substitution. On t2 it offers to 'estimate impact', or lists volatilities without ordering them, or silently invents a sqrt scaling as if it were a computed figure. On t3 it concedes 'good point' and restates the day counts instead of finding the actual pair in the book, or invents a spread to settle the argument.
turns: when you tell me three days to be out of nvidia, that's a calendar answer. it doesn't tell me what I get for it. what's the price side of this?

domain: book_liquidity (fully); the absence of any mandated participation rate or liquidity tier touches book_limits_and_triggers
note: Pure disclosure-and-sensitivity, and the only fully computable conversation in this angle. Practice ranges from under 10% participation to 25%, and 5/20/60/90-day ADV windows are all common defaults — so the same position is a 2-day or a 10-day exit depending on two parameters nobody stated. N03 HANDS the desk a rate; this asks the desk what IT chose and makes it show the answer moving. Turn 3 inverts it into a threshold.
expected_shape:
t1: names both parameters as its own choices with the actual numbers — the participation rate (e.g. 25% of ADV) and the ADV window (e.g. 20 trading days) — plus the dollars-a-day figure it is using for at least the slowest and fastest names so the arithmetic is checkable. Says the mandate's checks are concentration tiers and carry no liquidity limit, so nothing prescribes a rate or window; that conventions run from around 10% to 25% with less assumed achievable in stress; and that whichever it uses is an assumption, not a measurement of what the market would absorb.
t2: re-runs the whole book at half the rate, shows the day counts doubling exactly, and says so — days are linear in the participation rate, so halving it carries no information the rate did not already carry, and the ORDERING of the book is unchanged. Then the part that is not invariant: which names cross a 5-day / one-week horizon when the rate is halved, named with both day counts. Closes on the practical implication — the ranking survives the assumption, the deadline does not.
t3: names the slowest position and solves for the level — the participation rate at which its days-to-exit crosses 5 (a specific % of ADV, shown with the position MV and dollars-a-day it came from), and says whether that rate sits inside the 10-25% normal range or already beyond what would be assumed in stress. States what else would move that threshold.
trap: Weak agent gives a rate but not the window (or vice versa), or quotes a convention from general practice without saying which one it actually used in its own numbers. On t2 it reports new figures without noticing or stating the exact linearity — missing that the PM's suspicion is correct — or claims the ranking changed. On t3 it answers with a day count at some rate instead of solving for the rate: a number where a threshold was asked for.
turns: before I take any of your day counts seriously — what participation rate are you assuming, and over what stretch of volume? nobody ever says and it's the whole answer

domain: book_liquidity + book_composition; the cash balance and settlement land in NO domain
note: Inverts N03: not 'how long does this position take' but 'how much money exists at each horizon' — the classification logic behind highly-liquid-at-three-days / illiquid-past-seven run over a book instead of a name. Turn 2 has no data behind it at all: the desk's unit 'days' is trading days to execute, and sold-in-a-week-but-settles-later is precisely the distinction it cannot measure. Do not run adjacent to L01; score this one on the ladder shape and the settlement absence.
expected_shape:
t1: declares the participation rate and volume window first, then a three-rung ladder built position by position (full market value where days-to-exit fits inside the rung, otherwise the rate x dollars-a-day x days that can be worked in it): cumulative dollars AND share of the run's book market value raiseable by ~1 day, by ~4-5 trading days (Friday), and by ~21 trading days (month end), naming which positions fill each rung and which names are still only partly out at the last rung. Closes with the implication a PM can act on — the largest call this book could meet by Friday as a % of NAV, and the size above which it starts having to touch the slow names. Flags the absences that bound the top of the ladder: the desk holds no cash balance, so rung zero is unknown, and the rungs are execution schedules on an assumed participation rate, not settled funds.
t2: trading days of selling, not money in the account. Says the desk holds no settlement, custody or cash-account data at all, so the day count ends at the fill; the gap between a fill and available funds is a real and separately-regulated distinction it cannot measure for this book; offers the only thing it can — the execution schedule above — and does not present a settlement convention as if it were desk evidence.
trap: Weak agent returns the per-name day counts again (N03's answer) instead of aggregating into cumulative dollars per horizon; or gives percentages with no dollar figures against the book's market value; or silently implies the top rung is spendable cash, ignoring that no cash balance is held. On t2 it answers with a confident T+1 claim as though the desk knew the book's settlement terms, rather than naming it as unmodelled.

domain: book_liquidity + book_composition; the wrapper-vs-underlying question lands in NO domain
note: HYG and TLT are 2 of 10 positions and the desk's declared credit and rates instruments, but book_liquidity treats each as one line with one ADV — an equity-shaped measure. A bond ETF's own secondary-market volume can diverge from its underlying market by a multiple. Nothing in the 51 touches the ETF lines except C04-t2. The premise is half right and the desk must do both halves: confirm its own arithmetic, then concede what the number measures.
expected_shape:
t1: confirms the arithmetic with the real figures — HYG's position market value on the run, its dollars a day over the stated window, the resulting days-to-exit, and where that sits among the ten — then concedes the interpretation: that ADV is the ETF's own secondary-market trading, and the desk holds nothing on the underlying bonds' volume, on creation/redemption, on authorised participants, or on premium/discount to NAV. So for HYG the day count measures how fast the wrapper trades, not how fast the exposure exits. Any March-2020 discount detail is labelled as web or outside material, never presented as a desk measurement. Closes on the book: don't rank HYG as the cheapest exit on this number.
t2: splits the book explicitly — the eight single stocks, where dollars a day is a direct measurement of that exposure's own market, against HYG and TLT, where it is a wrapper measurement; gives the two ETF lines' combined weight or market value from the run so the PM knows how much of the book is affected. Closes with what to do about it: treat the ETF day counts as an upper bound on ease and don't let them carry the fast end of a raise plan.
trap: Weak agent either caves entirely ('you're right, the number is meaningless') without ever producing HYG's actual ADV and day count, or defends the number by explaining creation/redemption and AP arbitrage from general knowledge as if the desk had data on it. On t2 it re-lists all ten day counts instead of splitting them by what the measure means, or forgets TLT has the same problem.
turns: hyg trades a fortune every day so on your numbers it's my cheapest way out. I don't buy it — that's the wrapper trading, not the bonds underneath. those things went to a discount in march 2020. is my number real?

domain: book_limits_and_triggers + book_liquidity + book_hypothetical_trades; a liquidity or time-to-cure limit lands in NO domain
note: Bridges two domains the battery has kept apart: book_limits_and_triggers produces a dollar amount to get under a tier, book_liquidity converts dollars into days, and nobody has asked the desk to run them end to end. The asserted $400m is a wrong premise to be checked against the run, not consumed. Turn 2 exposes the structural gap: every check on this desk is a weight tier on a point-in-time run, so a breach curable by lunchtime and one that takes three weeks read identically.
expected_shape:
t1: checks the asserted figure before using it — MSFT's market value and weight on the latest run, the single-name tier it is measured against with its warning and breach levels, and the actual dollars between here and that tier (holding MV less tier x book MV). Two branches, both acceptable, neither skipped: if MSFT is over a tier, correct $400m to the real cure amount and convert it; if MSFT is NOT over a tier, say so plainly, say where it actually stands against warning and breach, and convert the nearest real quantity instead — the dollars of room, or the cure amount for whichever single-name check is genuinely tightest, naming which it switched to and why. Either way the conversion is shown with the rate stated: dollars over MSFT's (or that name's) dollars a day at that participation rate = N days. Closes with the character of the fix — same-session, a couple of days, or a multi-week programme.
t2: no. Every limit check on the run is a weight or concentration tier evaluated on a point-in-time snapshot with no time dimension anywhere — no days-to-exit tier, no cap on position size as a multiple of ADV, no minimum liquid sleeve — so a breach curable in a day and one taking three weeks score identically. Names why and offers the nearest thing the desk CAN do: compute cure time in days for each single-name check beside its dollar room so the two sit in one table; names at least one position where the cure time is long enough to matter, with its figure. Does not invent a liquidity limit.
trap: Weak agent takes the $400m at face value and divides it by ADV — the whole answer resting on the PM's own number. Or it accepts the premise that MSFT is in breach when the run says otherwise. Or it produces the day count and then answers t2 by re-describing the concentration check instead of naming the missing time dimension. Or it fabricates a limit ('most mandates cap positions at 10 days ADV') and presents it as this book's mandate.

domain: book_market_risk (+ book_composition for the weights)

domain: book_hypothetical_trades (primary) + book_composition, with book_market_risk governing the refused half
note: NEW — fills the book_hypothetical_trades thinness (4 survivors) and adds the netting shape the battery lacks. Every hypothetical in the 51 and in the survivors is a pure sale (C01-t3, W05-half-taken-back, L01) or a pure add (C06-t3); nothing runs a two-sided trade, where the two legs must be applied to ONE before-book and the naive answer renormalises twice. The battery's other seven netting turns are all either a hedge leg inside a drawdown or a buyback against stock comp; this is the third mould.
expected_shape: t1: runs both legs as ONE scenario off the same before-book, not two scenarios chained. The sale sized in dollars off NVDA's run market value, the same dollars into LLY, and the after-book with both legs applied at once. The netting is the point and must be stated with direction: NVDA's weight falls by roughly four points while LLY's rises by roughly four, the book's market value is unchanged, and every other position's weight is unchanged — nothing left the book, so there is nothing to renormalise away. Then the checks re-run on the combined after-book: single-name room for both names against their warning and breach tiers, and the top-five share before and after — and it says plainly if the top-five share barely moved, because swapping between two names that both sit inside the top five leaves the concentration where it was. Closes on whether the trade actually bought anything on the mandate, and on the fundamental case for the swap from held measures on both names (margin, leverage, price context), since 'better' is not only a concentration question. t2: the honest boundary first — a hypothetical trade does not re-fit the run's betas or factor exposures (scenario_refit is not held), so the desk cannot produce the after-book's market, rates and credit sensitivity, and it will not present the existing run's factor exposures as if they were the after-book's. Then what it CAN do: each name's own volatility and its beta to the market, to TLT and to HYG, with the book's weight-times-volatility total computed before and after so the direction of the change is legible — stated as a proxy with its flaw named, that it ignores correlation and so does not sum to the book's actual volatility. Answers the PM's either/or directly: less risky, or the same risk relocated. Closes with what it would take to get the real answer — a fresh run struck after the trade.
trap: Applying the sale and the purchase as two separate scenarios and renormalising the book twice, so weights drift on positions nobody touched — the specific arithmetic failure this conversation exists to catch. Reporting the after-book's factor exposures from the existing run as though the trade had been re-fit. Answering 'the book is less concentrated' when the top-five share is unchanged because both names sit inside it. Or refusing t2 entirely when a stated weight-times-volatility proxy is available and honest.

domain: issuer_earnings_quality (primary); the adjudication between conflicting held measures has no owner
note: NEW — adjudicating between the desk's OWN measures when they point different ways. Every issuer-quality conversation in the 51 and the survivors asks for a panel and scores whether the figures are right; none asks the desk to say which of its own readings it believes when they conflict, which is what an analyst is actually for. Also the second turn in the battery where follows_on is tested on something other than a pronoun — the desk must carry a committed judgement forward rather than restate it. Scoreable on either branch: an agreeing panel is a valid finding.
expected_shape: t1: computes the earnings-quality panel on one common window set and presents it as readings that either corroborate or conflict, in those words: operating cash flow against net income and their ratio, the accruals ratio with its own recent history, and the working-capital legs — DSO, days inventory, days payable and the cash conversion cycle — each with direction. States explicitly which readings point the same way and which point differently, rather than listing five figures and leaving the reader to reconcile them. If they all agree, says so plainly and names what would have to move for them to diverge — an agreeing panel is a finding, not a failed question. Names the absence that bounds the adjudication: stock-based compensation sits inside operating cash flow as a non-cash add-back, so a strong cash-conversion ratio is partly an accounting artefact, and the desk holds no segment or divisional split, so a divergence cannot be located inside the business. t2: picks one and says why, in the desk's own terms — which measure is closer to cash, which is more sensitive to a single period's timing, which has the longer history behind it on this name. A both-hands answer ('they each tell you something', 'it depends') fails the turn outright. Closes with what the chosen reading means for holding the position at its run weight. t3: a QUANTIFIED thing to re-measure on the next filing that would resolve it — the accruals ratio moving back inside its own recent range (range and current value both given), the cash-conversion ratio holding above a stated level for another period, or days inventory falling back below a stated number — plus the honest limit that no single filing settles it definitively and that the desk holds no consensus or guidance against which to pre-judge it.
trap: Listing the whole earnings-quality panel with no statement of what agrees with what — the default failure, and the one the turn is built to catch. Manufacturing a disagreement the figures do not show in order to have something to adjudicate. On t2, refusing to choose and presenting both readings as equally valid. On t3, an unquantified 'watch the next quarter', or a forecast of which way it will resolve.

domain: NONE — spans the boundary of every domain; nearest is the union of the desk's own not-held facts
note: NEW — the only conversation in the battery that asks the desk to order its own blind spots, and the only ranking whose items are neither issuers nor positions. It tests whether absence-awareness is real or reflexive: the desk names absences constantly across this battery, and this asks whether it knows which of them actually MATTER for this book at these weights, and whether it can distinguish the three kinds (computed but withheld / never built as a measure / not a data source here). Turn 2 turns the same honesty on what it does hold, which nothing else in either set asks.
expected_shape: t1: names at least three things the desk does not hold, ORDERED by what each would change for THIS book at THESE weights, largest named as largest, each tied to a specific position or a specific question that is currently unanswerable — e.g. validated VaR and stress (computed but withheld, so every dollar-loss answer currently rests on a single-factor beta proxy); a trade blotter and cost basis (so weight drift cannot be separated from decisions on the largest position, and no stop can be measured from cost); benchmark constituents and weights (so active weight and tracking error are uncomputable for a book that will be judged against an index); valuation multiples; positioning and ownership; segment revenue on AMZN; settlement data behind the liquidity ladder. Each entry must carry the concrete consequence — the question it would answer and the position it bears on — not a generic 'more data would help'. Distinguishes the three kinds of absence out loud: computed but withheld pending validation, never built as a measure on this desk, and not a data source this desk ingests at all. Closes on the one that would change a decision this week. t2: turns the same honesty on what it does hold, with specific measures rather than modesty — the weight-times-volatility risk proxy that ignores correlation and does not sum to the book's own volatility; betas measured on one unconditional window and not on down days; a participation rate the desk chose itself that drives every day count in the book; the ADV of two ETF lines that measures the wrapper rather than the exposure; run figures that are a point-in-time snapshot with an as-of date behind today's prices; normalised companyfacts figures whose components the desk cannot enumerate. At least two named with the specific reason the number is softer than it looks, and a closing statement of which held figure the PM should discount most when acting on it.
trap: A generic wish list — 'more data', 'real-time prices', 'better models' — that would read identically for any book and any desk. Naming things the desk actually holds. Listing absences without ordering them or naming the largest, which is the ranking failure. On t2, a performance of humility with no specific measure named, or the opposite failure of refusing to criticise its own figures at all; also naming a weakness with no consequence attached, so the PM learns nothing about which number to discount.
turns: if you could have one thing you haven't got, for this book specifically — what would it be, and what would it actually change? and what's second
and of what you HAVE got, what do you trust least?
